news.title: Gun’s warning to English rivals; star’s emotional return, Kerr lives ‘American dream’: Tillies Tracker
news.lede: With the Women’s Super League kicking off this weekend, crunch time has arrived for the Matildas ahead of next year’s FIFA World Cup in Brazil. The global showpiece tournament begins next June and Australia’s stars will need to be in top form for their respective clubs to shake off the disappointment of March’s Asian Cup final loss to Japan in Sydney, and match the unforgettable run to the semi-finals on home soil in 2023. Not all of the Matildas’ big names are plying their trade in England this season, but the core of Joe Montemurro’s team will be using the world’s biggest league as their World Cup launch pad.

news.title: Football Legends and the Power of World Cup Nostalgia
news.lede: The 2026 World Cup has come to an end, and there is good reason people are talking about what a success it was. Revenues are estimated to be between USD 13.5 billion and USD 15 billion for the entire 2023–2026 cycle, surpassing the USD 11 billion expectation for this period. Another of the hottest talking points was the “Americanization” of the tournament featuring the “4 quarters” due to controversial hydration breaks, the halftime show at the final, and shots of celebrities in the stands during the broadcast, all typical of U.S. sports. In addition to the FIFA president, who appeared in broadcasts during the 9th minute of every match, the legends stole the spotlight.

news.title: Key investor Kushner blames football power struggle for World Cup plan collapse
news.lede: Investor Joshua Kushner has blamed power struggles within global football for the outrage over Fifa’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup, admitting his firm “would not have gotten involved” if it had anticipated the backlash. The first comments by venture capitalist Kushner – the brother of Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump – since the plan collapsed came on Monday, as European governing body Uefa prepares a criminal case against Fifa president Gianni Infantino. “While we stand behind the motivations of FFE [Fifa Forward Enterprise], we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to,” Kushner said in a statement.
